selected.name: Off-screen narrative
selected.instruction: Give 10 when the caption implies a specific unseen event, history, or consequence that makes the pictured moment newly funny; give 0 when it adds no temporal or narrative information.
selected.rationale: R21 implies an earlier change in the flock, R24 implies a failed engagement, and R35 implies a long accident-free period. These captions make the static image feel like part of a larger story.
member_names: Implied unseen backstory beyond the depicted moment
Implies an off-panel history or consequence
Introduces an outside fact that recontextualizes the frame

selected.name: Comic economy: punch lands with minimal, load-bearing words
selected.instruction: Score how tightly compressed the caption is in achieving its comedic effect, with essentially no throat-clearing, hedging, or explanatory padding, ending on the load-bearing punch word. 10 = extremely compressed, every word necessary, caption ends on the punch; 0 = padded or explanatory phrasing dilutes or delays the punch.
selected.rationale: R24 ('it's so ewe') delivers its full pun in four words with the punch as the final word; R33 ('you need to get your act together') is a short line that ends precisely on the double-meaning word 'act'. Both dense_high_card_low (dense .981/.991 vs card .159/.272), consistent with the dense model rewarding tight compression that a criterion-by-criterion scorecard may not specifically credit.
member_names: Comic economy: punch lands with minimal, load-bearing words

selected.name: Idiom-to-Visual Binding
selected.instruction: Score how perfectly a common idiom, saying, or stock phrase is rendered literal or physical by the specific content of the drawing. A 10 means a familiar dead phrase springs back to life because the drawing makes it literally true in a new way. A 0 means no idiom is present, or the idiom is used figuratively with no visual reinforcement.
selected.rationale: R19 ('pull the wool over my eyes' — a wolf literally trying on a wool costume) and R52 ('get your act together' — a circus 'act' is physically parading through) show the dense model rewarding captions where the drawing resurrects a cliché, a mechanism a text-only scorecard may not distinguish from ordinary punning.
member_names: Idiom/cliché literalized onto a specific visual detail
Pre-existing idiom literalized by the drawing
Stock phrase or lyric literalized by the drawing, unnamed

selected.name: Conversational Deadpan Delivery
selected.instruction: Score 10 if the caption mimics a completely mundane, casual remark or complaint that sharply contrasts with the absolute chaos or surrealism of the drawing; score 0 if the tone is melodramatic, exclamatory, or explicitly acknowledges the weirdness.
selected.rationale: The juxtaposition of a casual tone with a chaotic scene is a classic contest technique. R10 ('he got indicted') and R46 ('you're rambling again') rank incredibly high for the dense model because they treat the surreal parade with deadpan casualness, a nuance the scorecard appears to miss.

selected.name: Novel interpretive angle
selected.instruction: Give 10 when the caption finds a surprising but defensible angle instead of the most obvious observation or stock pun; give 0 when it is predictable, generic, or simply restates the premise.
selected.rationale: R14 applies a contemporary consent dispute to the mosquito scene, R31 makes kitchen security depend on family misfortune, and R45 uses a conventional animal joke. The first examples demonstrate more distinctive angles.

selected.name: Phonetic pun precision
selected.instruction: Score 10 when a sound-alike or word-form substitution is exact, immediately decipherable, and image-specific; score 0 when the pun is strained, obscure, or detachable from the cartoon.
selected.rationale: Rows R24, R39, and R49 demonstrate compact sound or spelling transformations tied to piano, bird, and sheep imagery.

selected.name: Two-reading semantic fit
selected.instruction: Score 10 when one phrase supports both a literal reading and an idiomatic or conceptual reading, with both fitting the cartoon; score 0 when only one unforced meaning is present.
selected.rationale: Rows R04, R06, and R23 use “cross word,” “keys,” or “gravity” so the wording operates simultaneously in the caption and the image.

selected.name: Macabre or Edgy Subtext
selected.instruction: Score 10 if the caption confidently extracts a dark, morbid, or highly inappropriate implication from an otherwise mundane or silly visual; score 0 if the caption is sanitized, overly safe, or points out the obvious absurdity instead of the dark implication.
selected.rationale: The dense model rewards captions that find the darkest or most transgressive angle of a drawing. R32 ('my dad lost a leg' regarding kitchen bear traps) and R47 ('exposed skin implies consent' regarding a mosquito) score high for the dense model but low for the scorecard, likely because the scorecard penalizes edgy humor.
member_names: Purposeful edgy/taboo content (sexual, dark, or transgressive)

selected.name: Salient-detail integration
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the caption makes two or more conspicuous visual details interact in one joke; score 0 when it could fit a generic version of the scene and ignores its specifics.
selected.rationale: Rows R08, R23, and R55 connect multiple visible elements into a single comic mechanism rather than merely naming the absurd premise.

selected.name: Adapted familiar phrase
selected.instruction: Score 10 when a recognizable idiom, lyric, or saying is minimally altered so that its new wording fits the depicted situation; score 0 when a familiar phrase is merely pasted onto the scene.
selected.rationale: R10 and R11 adapt “coming round the mountain”; R45 transforms “pull the wool over my eyes” for the wolf costume.

selected.name: Metaphorical or Satirical Mapping
selected.instruction: Score 10 if the caption brilliantly maps the surreal visual elements to a recognizable real-world concept (e.g., a political process, social dysfunction, or bureaucracy) without over-explaining the connection; score 0 if the caption is entirely literal or misses the chance for metaphor.
selected.rationale: The dense model highly ranks captions that require the reader to bridge a visual absurdity to a real-world concept. Row R10 ('he got indicted') and R37 ('republican primary ticket') rank very high for the dense model but low for the scorecard, suggesting the scorecard misses these clever, cynical metaphorical mappings.
member_names: Reframes the whole scene as public or institutional life

selected.name: Social-norm inversion
selected.instruction: Give 10 when a recognizable social rule or institution becomes the mechanism that explains the cartoon’s absurdity; give 0 when no social norm is involved or the topical reference is merely attached.
selected.rationale: R14 turns a social norm about exposed skin into the mosquito’s defense, R24 turns metal detection into relationship suspicion, and R60 turns personal-space etiquette into the island encounter. The humor arises from applying ordinary norms in extraordinary settings.

selected.name: Meta-humor about the joke/genre itself
selected.instruction: Score how much the caption comments on the act of joke-telling, the contest genre, or the comedic convention of noticing absurdity, rather than staying purely inside the depicted scene. 10 = the caption knowingly winks at its own status as a joke or at the reader's/judge's expectations; 5 = a mild self-aware aside; 0 = the caption is entirely diegetic with no self-reference.
selected.rationale: R14 ('i'll bet they can't even detect irony') turns the cartoon's metal-detector search into a comment on the caption's own ironic mode; R01 ('you're rambling again') reads as commentary on rambling/verbosity itself, functioning independent of any specific cartoon content. Both are dense_high_card_low (dense .859/.991 vs card .353/.474).

selected.name: Dark or transgressive content delivered deadpan
selected.instruction: Score for content that is morbid, bodily, sexual, or ethically uncomfortable, delivered in a flat conversational register with no apology or wink. 10 = genuinely edgy material said as though it were small talk. 5 = mildly impolite. 0 = entirely wholesome content, or edgy content that is signposted, leering, or delivered with visible relish. Score the presence and deadpan handling of the transgression; do not penalize the caption for being impolite and do not reward mere shock without the flat delivery.
selected.rationale: R10 ('you should see the breasts'), R18 ('where we disagree is that exposed skin implies consent'), R26 ('my dad lost a leg') and R30 ('we'll be pooped by the end of the night') are all dense-high with very low card percentiles (0.042, 0.134, 0.076, 0.040), a pattern consistent with a bank that contains a tastefulness or appropriateness term suppressing exactly the material the dense model rewards.
member_names: Dark content delivered in a placid register
Dark or transgressive content delivered deadpan

selected.name: Punchline Unpredictability
selected.instruction: Score how surprising the caption's meaning or ending is given the visual setup. A 10 means the caption arrives at a destination no reasonable person would predict from the drawing, yet it makes perfect sense in hindsight. A 0 means the punchline is the most obvious or expected first-thought response.
selected.rationale: R01 (indictment for a circus — utterly unexpected) and R43 ('lost a leg' — the escalation from '45 pounds' is shocking) show the dense model crediting surprise, while dense_low items like R07 ('we had to catch our own fish') and R17 ('eat my dessert first') are highly predictable responses the scorecard may over-credit for straightforward relevance.

selected.name: Generic well-formed complete-sentence 'caption-shaped' joke
selected.instruction: 0-10: how much does the caption read as a fully-formed, grammatically complete, self-contained joke sentence with a clear setup-and-punchline shape that would be recognizable as 'a good caption' even to someone who has never seen this particular drawing, versus a fragment, an oblique aside, or a line that only makes sense once you already know the specific scene? 0 = incomprehensible or meaningless without the specific drawing; 10 = polished, complete, self-contained joke sentence that reads as generically caption-shaped. Score only this generic well-formedness; do not judge whether it is actually the best caption for this drawing.
selected.rationale: R46 ('no bag--my cubs still think i catch my own salmon', dense_pct=0.338/card_pct=0.991) and R49 ('when i was a kid, we had to catch our own fish', dense_pct=0.452/card_pct=0.968) are both polished, complete, self-contained jokes that any generic reader would flag as 'a good caption,' and both are strongly card-favored while only dense-middling — showing generic well-formedness can be scored highly by a criterion bank without being what most distinguishes fit to this particular cartoon.
member_names: Generic caption-shaped joke: scaffolded setup with tidy payoff

selected.name: Terse fragment/staccato delivery
selected.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how much the caption is delivered as short clipped fragments (very few words, punctuated as separate short bursts rather than one flowing sentence) rather than as a longer flowing sentence. 0 = long flowing single sentence with no internal breaks; 10 = extremely short, broken into staccato fragments/repeated short bursts. Score only the extent of this fragment/staccato quality present in the wording and punctuation; do not judge whether the caption is funny or good.
selected.rationale: R15 ('six feet dude. six. feet', dense_pct=0.040/card_pct=0.953) and R43 ('honey, the remote is in your hand', dense_pct=0.225/card_pct=0.947) are terse/clipped and card-favored while dense ranks them low; a longer flowing line like R37 ('where we disagree is that exposed skin implies consent', dense_pct=0.859/card_pct=0.134) is dense-favored instead — brevity/rhythm is a stylistic tell, not per-cartoon fit.

selected.name: Transcription and typography conventions of the compiled list
selected.instruction: MODE 4 fingerprint. Score 0-10 for how much NON-DEFAULT TYPOGRAPHY the caption carries relative to the plain lowercase unpunctuated norm of this list. Add extent for: terminal punctuation present (a final period, question mark or exclamation); internal sentence-final periods splitting the line; quotation marks around an embedded phrase; double-hyphen or dash constructions; ellipses; digits written as numerals; symbols that appear stripped or mangled (a percentage or currency sign missing beside a number); any capitalisation at all. 0 = all lowercase, no terminal punctuation, no marks beyond a single comma; 10 = several of these conventions at once. You must NOT judge whether the punctuation is correct, careful or sloppy; count only how much marked typography is visible.
selected.rationale: MODE 4: whoever compiled and normalised these entries left an uneven trace, and the unevenness is legible. R58 carries both quotation marks and a terminal period ('good girl.'), R59 uses a double hyphen (no bag--my cubs), R50 reads 100 wool with the percentage sign evidently lost in transcription, R28 carries a bare numeral (581 days), R54 uses sentence-final periods for emphasis (six. feet), while the great majority of rows such as R41, R11 and R14 are bare lowercase with no terminal mark. None of this is a property of the joke's fit to the drawing, but it is trivially learnable from raw text.

selected.name: Datable era idiom fixing the entry to a period
selected.instruction: MODE 3 fingerprint. Score 0-10 for how strongly the caption's wording DATES it to a specific stretch of years, independent of any political content. Look for: pandemic-era idiom (distancing measures such as six feet, herd immunity, closures and shutdowns of restaurants or venues, masking, remote work); named consumer technology and platforms of a given moment (iphone, streaming, apps, texting); slang and address terms whose currency rises and falls (dude, hysterical); and conversely idiom that reads as older-register (telegram, party line). 0 = wording that would read the same in any decade; 5 = one mildly period-flavoured word; 10 = the caption cannot be understood without knowing what was happening in one particular year or two. You must NOT judge whether the dated reference is stale, fresh, or well used; score only how tightly the wording pins a period.
selected.rationale: MODE 3: the actual contest date is invisible, but era leaves a lexical trace. Sharp examples inside the slice: R54 (six feet dude. six. feet), R17 (they claim they have herd immunity), R12 (the worst thing to temporarily shut down a restaurant) all carry pandemic-window idiom; R06 (no tv or iphone) pins a consumer-technology era. Era membership is a property of when the entry was written, not of how well it reads its cartoon, yet it is highly visible in the tokens and therefore learnable by any text model as a shortcut.

selected.name: Live-news political reference (news-cycle fingerprint)
selected.instruction: MODE 2 fingerprint. Score 0-10 for how much the caption depends on a REFERENCE TO CURRENT-EVENTS POLITICS or public-affairs news: named or implied parties, primaries, slates, tickets, candidates, votes and ballots, indictments, the White House, officeholders, campaigns, scandals. 0 = no political or civic content whatever; 3 = one glancing civic word that is not load-bearing; 7 = the joke's second meaning requires the reader to hold a political story in mind; 10 = the caption is nothing but the political reference. Judge only whether the political frame is present and how load-bearing it is. You must NOT judge whether the politics is timely, accurate, agreeable, tired or funny, and you must not form any view of the caption's merit.
selected.rationale: MODE 2(a): an unobservable upstream factor here is WHICH WEEK the contest ran and what was dominating the news then; MODE 2(b): its textual fingerprint is exactly this vocabulary. The slice is loaded with it and it clusters: R08 (republican primary ticket) and R15 (it's the republican slate of candidates) are the same reference twice for the same drawing, plus R47 (he got indicted), R48 (they're still looking for votes), R09 (our new white house collection). A political reference is a fact about the calendar, not about how well the line reads the drawing, and a text-only model can pick up the vocabulary while learning nothing about fit.
